sections.html:
West Haven is a shoreline city in New Haven County. The 2020 census counted 55,584 residents, and the city has 22,735 housing units, 5.8% of them vacant. Median household income was $73,566.

Where a house sits changes who is likely to buy it. Center, around the green and Campbell Avenue, is the main commercial street. West Shore runs along the water. Allingtown is the hilly district around the University of New Haven, and Sandy Point is a beach and bird sanctuary reaching into New Haven Harbor. A waterfront house and a hillside house near campus draw different people.

The city grew from 25,808 residents in 1930 to 52,851 in 1970, so a lot of the housing stock dates from those decades. Roofs, wiring and heating systems in houses that age are the first things a buyer's inspector will look at, and a seller is better off knowing their condition before the first showing.

sections.h2: Who values your property and who sends the bill
sections.html:
Two offices handle your tax. The Assessor's Office sets the value, and the Tax Collector sends the bill and takes payment. The Assessor's Office is in City Hall at 355 Main Street, 1st floor, phone 203-937-3515, open Monday to Friday from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Questions about value, exemptions and appeals go to the Assessor. Questions about what you owe today go to the Tax Collector. Mixing the two up is the most common reason a phone call goes nowhere, so write down which office you need before you dial.

The Assessor's site also posts a mill rates sheet and a street list sorted by fire district. Both are worth opening before you quote anyone a tax figure. Start at the Assessor's Office page.

Assessment topicWest Haven detail
Assessment level70% of fair market value
Most recent revaluationRevaluation 2024
Appeal bodyBoard of Assessment Appeals
Forms offeredAppeals application and representative form
Relief programsState elderly and totally disabled programs, military service exemptions, blind exemption, renters rebate
RecordsOnline assessment records and West Haven GIS

The assessed value on your bill is 70% of market value, so it will look lower than what you expect to sell for. That is normal and does not mean the house is underpriced.

An owner who thinks the value is wrong files with the Board of Assessment Appeals. The Assessor's page offers an application and a separate form for a representative who files on your behalf. Call the Assessor's Office for the current filing window before you plan around it.

If your home was revalued in 2024 and the bill jumped, start with the Revaluation Questions and Answers page the Assessor links. The vendor's taxpayer information site is linked there too. Look at the property record card first. A wrong square footage, bedroom count or lot size is easier to correct with a phone call than a formal appeal.

Bring photos and a recent appraisal or comparable sales if you have them. An appeal about condition is stronger with dated pictures than with a description.

sections.h2: Does your fire district change the bill?
sections.html:
It can. Part of a West Haven tax bill depends on the fire district a street is in. The Allingtown district was folded into the city. The two independent districts that remain, First Fire Taxation (Center) and West Shore, each levy their own rate.

Use the Assessor's street list by fire district to find your address, then check the mill rates sheet. To estimate a payoff, ask the Tax Collector which district and rates apply to the exact address and whether any district amount arrives as a separate bill from the city's.

Residents have talked about consolidating the districts, so ask whether anything is changing before you give a buyer a firm annual cost.

The Tax Collector's office will give you the exact due dates, late-payment interest and the balance on your parcel. Call before you sign a sale agreement and ask for the figures in writing:

  • the real estate tax balance on the parcel, including any fire district amount;
  • the date each installment is due and what is already paid;
  • any sewer or other charge sitting on the property record;
  • the last day a payoff figure is good, so the closing date does not strand a few days of interest.

Keep that written payoff with your sale paperwork. The title company or closing attorney will ask for the same numbers, and having them early shortens the last week before closing.

The seller files Connecticut Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded. State tax is due when the price is $2,000 or more unless an exemption applies. West Haven's town code on the form is 156.

  • The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files the return.
  • Participating towns can use the state's myCTREC portal, and the payment is drawn only after recording.
  • Towns without electronic filing receive both pages of the form and a check made out to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

The state also lists an exemption for a principal residence sold for too little to pay the mortgages plus the real estate tax and other liens ahead of them, and another for a principal residence deeded in lieu of foreclosure. Your closing attorney picks the right code. The DRS conveyance tax page lists every exemption.

Unpaid property tax does not stop a sale. It does need to be settled at the closing table. A workable order of steps looks like this:

  1. Ask the Tax Collector for a written payoff that shows every open balance on the parcel.
  2. Send the figure to your closing attorney or title company before the contract is signed.
  3. Have the payoff listed on the settlement statement so it comes out of your proceeds.
  4. After closing, keep a copy of the paid receipt in case a question comes up later.

A cash buyer can work with a balance like this too, since title and tax status are checked either way. What slows things down is a surprise, such as a district charge nobody asked about. Asking early removes that risk.

sections.h2: Papers to gather before you list
sections.html:
A short folder of documents makes every conversation with a buyer, agent or attorney go faster.

  • Your deed and the most recent tax bill.
  • The property record card from the Assessor's online records.
  • Receipts or dates for major work on the roof, wiring and heating.
  • Any letters about exemptions or relief programs you currently receive.

If you receive an elderly, disabled or veterans exemption, tell your buyer it belongs to you and will not carry over automatically. They will need to apply on their own.

faqs.q: Who do I call about West Haven property assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Assessor's Office at 203-937-3515. It is on the first floor of City Hall at 355 Main Street and is open Monday to Friday from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

faqs.q: What percent of value does West Haven assess?
faqs.a: Property is assessed at 70% of fair market value. The most recent revaluation is Revaluation 2024.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal a West Haven assessment?
faqs.a: Appeals go to the Board of Assessment Appeals. The Assessor's page offers an application and a representative form, and the office can tell you the current filing window.

faqs.q: Does a fire district add to a West Haven tax bill?
faqs.a: It can. The two remaining independent fire districts each levy their own rate, and the Assessor posts a street list by fire district. Ask the Tax Collector which one applies to your address.

faqs.q: Can I sell a West Haven house that owes property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Get a written payoff from the Tax Collector, and the title company can pay the tax from the sale proceeds at closing.
